title: Ты же слово дал!  (You Gave Your Word!)

segments.t: Back at the town hall, Arkady has just finished a phone call planning City Day, with free beer and pop stars from Moscow, all to win votes. Last time, Samson's wife told him he should have accepted the mayor's job offer, silly, humiliating condition and all, so now Samson is back in the mayor's office. Let's listen in Russian first.
Ну, как хочешь. Лидия Алексеевна, зайдите, пожалуйста!
Мир, мир. А когда на работу?
Слушай, Самсон, я тут подумал. Твой начальник — такой опытный специалист.
Мы не можем его уволить. Это нехорошо.
А ты иди на биржу труда. Там есть работа.
А что я за мэр такой, который держит своё слово?
Let's go back through it slowly. Arkady has just sent a visitor away when he notices Samson standing at the door, and he's not exactly welcoming.
, with just a little sound of surprise before it. Then a short, rather cold question.
'What have you come for?' the expression for 'what for' is
. The action word translates to 'came', which is
, and it has an ending for a man, matching Samson's gender. Samson answers with just two words.
'Just once.' It begins with the Russian word meaning 'one', which is
. He means he'll do it, but only one time. Arkady pretends not to understand that's it.
'What do you mean, once?' He simply repeats Samson's words with the translation for 'what', which is
, in front. This makes Samson spell it out.
'Well, the thing you said.' He means the humiliating kiss Arkady demanded as the price of the job. The action word translates to 'said', which is
, with meaning 'you' in front. Arkady shrugs and calls someone in.
'Well, as you like.' The action word translates to 'you want', which is
. It's a handy phrase whenever you leave a choice to someone else. Then he calls his secretary.
'Lidia Alekseyevna, come in, please!' the expression meaning 'come in' is
, which is the polite form, the one you use with a boss, a stranger, or an older colleague. Samson doesn't like the idea of an audience.
'What's that for?' The same word for 'what for' as before, plus a little word for 'that', which translates to
'So that there are witnesses, Samson.' The opening term translates to 'so that', which is
. He wants proof that the deal is done. And so it happens, off stage. Afterwards, Arkady turns to his secretary.
'Lidia Alekseyevna, did you see everything?' He uses the expression meaning 'everything', which is
, and the polite form of 'you' with her, as he always does. She answers like a perfect secretary.
'Yes, Arkady Borisovich. I saw everything.' She calls her boss by his first name and his father's name, which is the respectful way. The action word translates to 'saw', which is
, and it has a feminine ending because she is a woman. Arkady is pleased.
'Now we're at peace.' The last word is
, which literally translates to both 'peace' and 'the world'. Samson echoes it straight back.
'Peace, peace.' He's not really interested in
, though. He has only one question on his mind.
'So when do I start work?' This literally translates to 'and when to work?', using the translation for 'when', which is
. The language often drops the action word when the meaning is clear. Now Arkady has something to tell him.
'Listen, Samson, I've been thinking.' The action word translates to 'thought', which is
, and it has an ending for a man in the past, marked by the 'l' sound.
'Your boss is such an experienced specialist.' the expression for 'experienced' is
. There's no equivalent for 'is' in it, as the language simply leaves it out in the present. This is the very boss Samson phoned and insulted the day before.
Мы не можем его уволить. Это нехорошо.
'We can't fire him. It's not nice.' The first sentence literally translates to 'we cannot him fire'. The action word for 'fire' is
. Little words like 'him' often move to the middle. Samson finally sees where this is going.
'Then what am I going to be?' the expression meaning 'what' translates to
, and it takes a special ending here, because it is about a job or a role you will have. Arkady has a suggestion.
А ты иди на биржу труда. Там есть работа.
'You go to the job centre. There's work there.' The first action word translates to 'go', which is
. It's a cruel joke: the mayor sends his old enemy to look for work like anyone else. Samson can't believe it.
'But you gave your word!' The little word after 'you' is
, which adds force, something built from the idea of 'but you did'. And here comes Arkady's answer.
А что я за мэр такой, который держит своё слово?
'And what kind of mayor would I be if I kept my word?' He uses meaning 'holds' or 'keeps', which is

, turning the normal idea of an honest politician upside down, on purpose. So the promise was revenge, not a job offer, just as he swore as a boy. Right, let's hear the whole scene again from the beginning.
Ну, как хочешь. Лидия Алексеевна, зайдите, пожалуйста!
Мир, мир. А когда на работу?
Слушай, Самсон, я тут подумал. Твой начальник — такой опытный специалист.
Мы не можем его уволить. Это нехорошо.
А ты иди на биржу труда. Там есть работа.
А что я за мэр такой, который держит своё слово?
That's it for this one. If the vocabulary felt heavy, don't worry: just listen out for the cry about giving your word, and Arkady's cheeky answer. See you next time!
